A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PIC task formulation, PIC-Bench benchmark and PIC-LM framework. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original PIC-Bench evaluations, training ablations, instruction-following measurements and downstream experiments on ASQA, Birthplace, QAMParI and BioASQ.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds human validation, robustness checks, general language evaluations, output analyses and training experiments at additional model sizes.

M1.justification: The original SFT, claim perturbation, probability-drop preference selection and length-normalized DPO procedure remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1. Section C.7 adds a 70B PIC-LM trained using QLoRA, a limited training adaptation beyond the original full-parameter implementation.

E1.justification: v2 adds MMLU, ARC-Challenge, GSM8K and AlpacaEval 2.0 evaluations in Section C.5.1 and Table 28, extending coverage to general knowledge, reasoning, mathematics and general instruction quality. The original PIC tasks, downstream datasets and biomedical evaluation are retained.

E2.justification: Corresponding PIC-Bench, few-shot, thinking-mode, BioASQ, RAG, pipeline and loss-ablation comparisons retain their comparator membership. Added studies reuse previously evaluated models, including Llama sizes already examined in v1's scaling analysis. The additional GPT-4.1 and Claude judges are evaluation backbones.

E3.justification: v2 introduces alternative-judge and alternative-prompt protocols, human extraction and verification studies with 120 and 72 samples and three annotators, and blinded linguistic comparisons. It also adds five-shot MMLU/GSM8K evaluation and training configurations at 1B, 3B and 70B, using QLoRA at 70B. Existing benchmark settings and 8B training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test evaluator agreement with humans, judge and prompt sensitivity, perturbed-response quality, and last-20-token versus whole-response preference scoring. Sections C.5.2 and C.7 additionally examine coherence, fluency, output errors and training scalability. These substantially expand validation beyond the retained training, reasoning-mode, domain-shift and downstream ablations.

E5.justification: Section B.4 adds exact inter-annotator agreement and Fleiss' kappa, including a verification kappa of 0.694. The existing 1,000-replicate bootstrap confidence intervals, instruction-following standard errors and three-seed preference-validation procedure remain unchanged; v2 does not establish an increase in repeated training runs.

E6.justification: The matched original numerical tables remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results from validation, robustness, linguistic analysis and model scaling. Examples include 81.0% human-verifier agreement and 93.2% average F1 for the new 70B PIC-LM. Table 28 also reports general-task tradeoffs: PIC-LM scores 69.3 versus its parent's 75.7 on GSM8K and 17.1 versus 20.9 on AlpacaEval.

T1.justification: The well-formedness assumptions, full/partial PIC definitions, support relation, precision/recall calculations, probability-drop formula and training objectives are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical results or proofs, and the added empirical analyses introduce no substantive mathematical revision.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and discussion retain the same central contributions and headline findings: PIC formulation, the eight-task benchmark, improved 8B grounding and downstream factuality benefits. Replacing intrinsic/extrinsic terminology with faithfulness/factuality largely preserves the intended claims; additional validation does not redefine them.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning preference-score length bias, the usefulness of imperfect preference samples, evaluator robustness and output error patterns. It refines the discussion of input fidelity and safety tradeoffs. However, the relocated limitations section omits v1's explicit warning about GPT-4o-mini evaluation errors and Prometheus generalization.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the scoring window as L=20, names OLMES for general evaluations, documents QLoRA for the 70B extension, and supplies alternative prompts and human-rating instructions. It also reports relative costs for additional judges. Original training details and artifact-access information are retained.

R1.justification: The relocated related-work section expands PIC's distinction from RAG and attributable generation. References are added for the new benchmarks, QLoRA, OLMES, the Delta Learning Hypothesis and output analyses. Two references concerning evaluator limitations are removed with that discussion; the main research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: v2 substantially edits and compresses the main narrative, changes hallucination terminology throughout, and moves Related Work and Limitations into Sections A.2 and A.3. It reorganizes appendix subsections and adds a NeurIPS checklist. These are substantial structural and editorial changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven tables covering judge and prompt checks, human validation, general performance, linguistic quality, errors and training scalability. Figure 1 receives revised colors, labels and arrows, while main Tables 3 and 5 become narrower displays wrapped by text. Most existing appendix displays are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the evidence through human validation and judge/prompt checks, while exposing output errors and general-task regressions that improve transparency. These gains are tempered by small validation studies and unexplained score inconsistencies: Table 8 reports PIC-LM averages of 89.9/91.2 under GPT-4o mini, versus 91.0/93.3 in Tables 2–3. Removing the explicit evaluator limitations also weakens qualification. The net improvement is useful but limited.
